title: Density, distribution and the factors behind them

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: What population density and population distribution mean, and the physical and economic factors that push each of them up or down.

blocks.heading: Density and distribution are different
blocks.text: Population density is the number of people per unit area, people per square kilometre, worked as total population divided by area: a district of 120 000 people on 300 square kilometres has 120 000 / 300 = 400 per square kilometre. Population distribution is different: it is where people live and where they do not, the pattern of spread. A distribution answer describes the pattern, dense along the river, thin in the north-west, and does it without listing place name after place name.

blocks.heading: The physical factors, each with its direction
blocks.text: Every physical factor must be linked to the way it pushes density. Steep relief makes farming and building hard, so density is low on high mountains; flat, fertile lowland grows crops and carries roads, so density is high. Reliable rain and rivers raise density, because crops and drinking water are secure, while dry climates lower it, because neither crops nor herds can live off the land. The error to avoid is naming a factor without saying which way it pushes: "the relief" is not an answer until it says low density here, high density there, and why.

blocks.heading: The economic and human factors
blocks.text: Jobs, ports and trade routes raise density, because people settle where the work and the markets are, and a city on a good harbour pulls in trade and the people who serve it. Poor access thins a population out, because goods and travellers pass it by, and weak soils and few jobs do the same. Physical factors set the stage and economic factors move the people: a desert oasis can grow if a mine opens, and a fertile valley can empty if its road closes.

blocks.heading: Causes are not consequences
blocks.text: A sparse population is caused by physical and economic factors: relief, climate, water, soils, access and jobs. A shortage of services is not one of the causes, because it comes after the emptiness: the few people cannot support schools and clinics, so the services thin out too. The test is whether the factor came before the sparse population or because of it.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: Density is the people of topic 1.1 spread over the ground, and the case studies below pair a dense area, the Ganges delta in Bangladesh, with a sparse one, the Namib coast of Namibia. Distribution also feeds the settlement patterns of topic 1.5.
